Tsukuba is written. === Chuzenji === '''Chuzenji'' (Chuzenji) is a Muhonji temple {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} of the {{ill|lt=Shingon sect|Q550182|WD=Q550182|1=Shingon Buddhism}} that existed in the area centered around the worship hall of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. {{ill|lt=Mountain name|Q11058522|WD=Q11058522|1=sangō}} is Mt. Tsukuba, and the temple name is Chisoku-in. The principal image is {{ill|lt=Senju Kannon|Q10904910|WD=Q10904910|1=Thousand-armed Kannon}}. It was also the 25th temple of {{ill|lt=Bando Thirty-Three Kannon|Q806417|WD=Q806417|1=Bandō Sanjūsankasho}} {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. It is said to have started with {{ill|lt=Tokuichi|Q7813728|WD=Q7813728|1=Tokuitsu}}, a monk of the {{ill|lt=Hosso sect|Q349849|WD=Q349849|1=East Asian Yogācāra}}, who opened ``Tsukubasan-dera''. is also found in "{{ill|lt=Genkoshasho|Q4153225|WD=Q4153225|1=Genkō Shakusho}}" of {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}} {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Its founding year is the first year of {{ill|lt=Enryaku|Q1373176|WD=Q1373176|1=Enryaku}} ({{ill|lt=782 years|Q30550|WD=Q30550|1=782}}) , Enryaku era (782-{{ill|lt=806|Q30021|WD=Q30021|1=806}}) {{Sfn|Chuzenji ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}, {{ill|lt=Tencho|Q1373138|WD=Q1373138|1=Tenchō}} first year ({{ill|lt=824|Q30353|WD=Q30353|1=824}}) {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba-san Shrine|1984|p=416}}, Tencho era (824-{{ill|lt=834|Q30381|WD=Q30381|1=834}}) {{Sfn|Tsukubasan-jinja Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}, etc.With the opening of Tsukuba-san Temple, the two deities of Mt. Tsukuba, male and female, came to be enshrined as ``Mt. Tsukuba Ryobu Gongen,'' with Kannon as the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=real Buddha|1=UNKNOWN}} {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Since Mt. Tsukuba has been a place for mountain training since ancient times, temples gradually flourished after that, and the name of the temple is said to have come to be called Chuzen-ji ('''Mt. Tsukuba Chisoku-in Chuzen-ji'') {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. {{ill|lt=Middle Ages|Q12554|WD=Q12554|1=Middle Ages}} include Mt. Nikko ({{ill|lt=Rinnoji|Q1348249|WD=Q1348249|1=Rinnō-ji}}), Mt. Sagami Daisen ({{ill|lt=Oyama Afuri Shrine|Q11434713|WD=Q11434713|lt=Daisenji|1=Ōyama Afuri Shrine}}), and Izu Hasashiyu ({{jal Ink|Izusan Shrine|Q611460|Izusan Sansho Gongen}}), {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} is said to have been one of the leading {{ill|lt=Shugendo|Q1483875|WD=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}} sacred sites in the Kanto region. The charge was held by the Tsukuba clan, starting with Tameji Tsukuba (Myogen) {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}.The situation in the Middle Ages is not known, but in the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it was protected by the shogunate as a place of prayer for {{ill|lt=Kimon|Q11673539|WD=Q11673539|1=Kimon}}, and the temple flourished again {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|WD=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} abolished the Tsukuba clan from the Tsukuba mountain betto in {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185|1=Keichō}} 5th year ({{ill|lt=1600|Q6720|WD=Q6720|1=1600}}), appointed Yutoshi as the founder of the Chukyo era, and established the Keicho era. In 1602|Q6727}}, he donated 500 koku as a divine territory, and in 15 Keicho years ({{ill|lt=1610|Q6765|WD=Q6765|1=1610}}), he donated 500 koku as a temple territory. In addition, the third shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|Q314481|WD=Q314481|1=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} restored the two shrines on the mountaintop, and also built the main hall (Omido), three-storied pagoda, bell tower, tower gate, Shinkyo Bridge, and shrines within the precincts of Hie, Kasuga, and Itsukushima {{Sfn|Ruins of Chuzenji Temple (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Also, during the time of the fifth shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi|Q313745|WD=Q313745|1=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi}}, it was renamed ``''Gojiin'''', and the temple territory counted 1,500 koku {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. After that, it continued to develop as a sacred mountain throughout the Edo period, and the {{ill|lt=monzen town|Q10564515|WD=Q10564515|1=Monzen-machi}} also developed {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}.After the Meiji Restoration, due to the {{ill|lt=Haibutsu Kishaku|Q702298|WD=Q702298|1=Haibutsu kishaku}}, the functions of Chuzenji ceased, the halls and pagodas were destroyed except for some shrine buildings, and the ritual implements were scattered all over the place {{Sfn|Ruins of Chuzenji Temple (Heibonsha)|1982}}. In 1930 (1930|Q18787}}), '''{{ill|lt=Omido (Tsukuba City)|Q11435427|WD=Q11435427|lt=Omido|1=Ōmi-dō}}''' (Omido) was rebuilt as a temple of the {{ill|lt=Shingon sect Toyozan school|Q3077351|WD=Q3077351|1=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha}} to the southwest of the worship hall of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine, and it continues to this day. === Related locations === [[File:Rokusho-jinja Ruins (Tsukuba) keidai.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Ruins of Rokusho Shrine (Usui, Tsukuba City)}}{{Small|Satomiya ruins of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. }}]] [[File:Hachimanzuka-kofun (Tsukuba) zenkei.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|[[Hachimanzuka Tumulus (Tsukuba City)|Hachimanzuka Tumulus]] (Numata, Tsukuba City)}}]] === Ruins of Rokusho Shrine === : Located in Tsukuba City {{ill|lt=Usui (Tsukuba City)|Q17194126|WD=Q17194126|lt=Usui|1=Usui, Tsukuba}} ({{Coord|36|12|2.18|N|140|6|38.53|E|region:JP-08|name=Motosato Shrine Ruins of Rokusho Shrine}}). : Also known as ``Rokusho Kodaijingu Ruins.'' The site of Satomiya, now a closed shrine. ``Rokusho'' is a general term for the two shrines of Tsukuba's male and female gods and the four shrines of Setsusha {{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. It is said that in the past, there were two shrines dedicated to the male and female deities, a worship hall, a Zuishinmon gate, and a treasure trove.{{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} This Rokusho Shrine was closed in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}43 ({{ill|lt=1910|Q2075|WD=Q2075|1=1910}}), and the divine spirit was (Tsukuba City)|Q17209343|Kamigun}} It was enshrined in the {{ill|lt=Kakekage Shrine|Q17228464|WD=Q17228464|1=Kokage Shrine}} (Kakekageyama Shrine) in the {{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. : According to "Silk Shadow Mountain Shintokuki", in the 20th year of {{ill|lt=Enryaku|Q1373176|WD=Q1373176|1=Enryaku}} ({{ill|lt=801|Q30008|WD=Q30008|1=801}}), k|Sakanoue Tamuramaro|Q941979}} is said to have deposited horse harnesses, a treasured sword, and a divine mirror here on his way back from the Ezo conquest. {{Sfn|Ruins of Rokusho Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. When the torii gate collapsed in the 3rd year of the Meiji era ({{ill|lt=1870|Q7741|WD=Q7741|1=1870}}), a bronze mirror was unearthed, and it is said that there was an inscription on the mirror that read, ``Stone torii gate, Seii Taishogun Sakanoue Tamuramaro erected'' {{Sfn|Ruins of Rokusho Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. === {{ill|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus (Tsukuba City)|Q17218702|WD=Q17218702|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus|1=Hachimanzuka-kofun}} === : Located in Numata, Tsukuba City ({{Coord|36|12|23.54|N|140|4|41.24|E|region:JP-08|name=Hachimanzuka Tumulus}}). : Located at the southwest foot of Mt. Tsukuba, this is the largest {{ill|lt=kofun|Q1141225|WD=Q1141225|1=Kofun}} in the Tsukuba region. This is a {{ill|lt=keyhole-shaped tumulus|Q11268718|WD=Q11268718|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} with a length of 90 meters, and is thought to have been constructed in the first half of the {{ill|lt=6th century|Q8090|WD=Q8090|1=6th century}}. . Abeshiko no Mikoto of the first generation {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Kunizo|Q11602846|WD=Q11602846|1=Tsukuba Kunizo}}About Tsukuba Kunizo, "{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" In Tsukuba Gunjo, Tsukuba no Mikoto (Tsukuba Mikoto) was the reign of the 10th {{ill|lt=Emperor Sujin|Q333530|WD=Q333530|1=Emperor Sujin}}. He was dispatched to ``{{ill|lt=Sendai Kūjihonki|Q2716751|WD=Q2716751|1=Kujiki}}'' ``Kokuzohonki'' In Tsukuba Kunizojo, Akoshiiro no Mikoto, the grandson of Ninko Takami no Mikoto, was appointed as the successor of the 13th Emperor, {{ill|lt=Emperor Seimu|Q316672|WD=Q316672|1=Emperor Seimu}}. Regarding this, there is a theory that the genealogy goes as ``Oshinobu no Mikoto - Chikutan no Mikoto - Akuseiro no Mikoto'', and another theory that Chikutan no Mikoto was a pioneer and the first generation was Akuseiro no Mikoto {{Harv|Tsukuba Province (Kadokawa)|1983}}. It is said to be the tomb of Mt. Tsukuba, and its relationship with the rituals of Mt. Tsukuba has been pointed out {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubasan Shrine|1984|p=414}}. There are many other ancient tombs in addition to this one, located at the southern foot of Mt. The peak on the left is the summit of Mt. Nantai, the peak on the right is the summit of Mt. Nyotai, and the large torii gate can be seen on the mountainside. }}]] [[File:Tsukubasan-jinja ōtorii.JPG|thumb|right|200px|{{Center|Ōtorii}}]]'''Tsukubasan Shrine'' (Tsukubasan Shrine) is located in {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|WD=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba City|Q273863|WD=Q273863|1=Tsukuba}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba (Tsukuba City)|Q11602837|WD=Q11602837|lt=Tsukuba|1=Tsukuba}}. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinai Shrine|1=Shikinaisha|WD=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}} 1 shrine, 1 small shrine). {{ill|lt=Modern shrine rank system|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Old shrine rank|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=prefectural shrine|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}, and currently it is {{ill|lt=Beppon Shrine|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of {{ill|lt=Shrine Headquarters|Q908077|WD=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. === Overview === It is a shrine that enshrines {{ill|lt=Mt. Tsukuba|Q1754619|WD=Q1754619|1=Mount Tsukuba}}, which rises to the southwest of {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|WD=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}} in the northeastern part of the {{ill|lt=Kanto Plain|Q1124865|WD=Q1124865|1=Kantō Plain}}, as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}}, and the main shrine buildings are located in the following three locations. :* '''Mt. Nantai Main Hall'' - The summit of the west peak (Mt. Nantai, 871 meters above sea level). :* '''Mt. Nyotai Main Hall''' - The summit of the eastern peak (Mt. Nyotai, 877 meters above sea level.The elevation of Mt. Nyotai was revised from 876 meters in 1999.). :* '''Hotel'''' - Mountainside (270 meters above sea level). View both main shrines from a distance. Mt. Tsukuba is a double-eared peak consisting of a west peak and an east peak, and the main shrine of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine is located on each peak. The precincts are vast, with the shrine site extending over the 270 meter above sea level line (prayer hall) on the south side of Mt. Tsukuba, and its area is approximately 354 {{ill|lt=ha|Q35852|WD=Q35852|1=Hectare}}. A {{ill|lt=monzen town|Q10564515|WD=Q10564515|1=Monzen-machi}} is formed around the worship hall halfway up the south side. Generally speaking, ``Tsukubasan Shrine'' often refers to the area around this worship hall. To the west of the shrine is Miyawaki Station of {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Scenic Railway|Q11602894|WD=Q11602894|1=Tsukuba Scenic Railway}}'s {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Scenic Railway Tsukuba Cable Railway Line|Q6924212|WD=Q6924212|lt=Mt. Tsukuba Cable Car|1=Mount Tsukuba Cable Car}}, and there is also a trailhead, which is crowded with not only worshipers but also mountain climbers.Mt. Tsukuba has been deeply worshiped as a divine mountain ever since it appeared in ``{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}},'' and Mt. Tsukuba Shrine, which enshrines the divine spirit, was deeply revered by court nobles and samurai families. As for cultural properties, the long sword (Mei Yoshimune) has been designated as a national {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Property|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}, and several shrine buildings have been designated as tangible cultural properties by Ibaraki Prefecture and Tsukuba City. === Enshrined God === The main {{ill|lt=enshrined deity|Q11591100|WD=Q11591100|1=Saijin}} is the following two pillars: :* '''Tsukuba Otoko no Kami'' (Tsukuba Otokami, Tsukuba Otokami) :*: The god of Mt. Nantai. The personal god is '''{{ill|lt=Izanagi|Q813858|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi no Mikoto|1=Izanagi}}''' (Izanagi no Mikoto). :* '''Tsukuba Goddess''' (Tsukuba Goddess) :*: God of Mount Nyotai. The personal god is '''{{ill|lt=Izanami|Q682306|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami no Mikoto|1=Izanami}}'''. The {{ill|lt=Shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532|1=Shintai}} of the main shrine is a divine robe (kanmiso), which is replaced at the Gozakae Festival {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Official Website)|Tsukubasan Shrine History}}. In addition, in "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Meiji Shrine Journals|1=UNKNOWN}}" it is referred to as a divine mirror {{Sfn|Meiji Shrine Journals|1912}}. Since the two gods Izanago no Mikoto and Iza Shokuson got married and gave birth to many gods and domestic births, they are believed to have blessings such as matchmaking, marital harmony, family safety, child-bearing, and child rearing. It is also said to have blessings such as traffic safety and construction safety. === About the enshrined deity === Mt. Tsukuba is a double-eared peak consisting of Mt. Nantai and Mt. Nyotai, each of which is dedicated to a deity. It is said that because of the mountain's appearance, with its two peaks side by side, it was natural for two male and female ancestor deities to be enshrined here. "{{ill|lt=Hitachi Province Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" "Hitachi Province Fudoki" Tsukuba-gunjo (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). Regarding Mt. Tsukuba, writes that the west peak (Mt. Nantai) was so steep that climbing it was prohibited as it was considered a divine peak. On the other hand, Higashimine (Mt. Nyotai) is steep, but springs flow constantly in summer and winter, and it is said that men and women gathered there in spring and autumn to perform {{ill|lt=utagaki|Q610915|WD=Q610915|1=Utagaki}}. In this way, Mt. Nantai was considered a restricted area, while Mt. Nyotai was considered an open area, and at the time the Fudoki was compiled, their characteristics were already very different. Numerous ritual artifacts have also been discovered near Mt. Nyotai from the end of the 7th century to the 12th century {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba (Kadokawa)|1983}}. The name of the god is written in {{ill|lt=Rokukokushi|Q1151168|WD=Q1151168|1=Rikkokushi}} as ``Tsukuba male god'' and ``Tsukuba goddess.'' In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, there were some theories that posited a personal god, and the following description can be found in the literature:{{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubasan Shrine|1984|p=414}}* Ichishasha {{ill|lt=Yamato Takeru|Q461258|WD=Q461258|lt=Nihon Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, Ichishasha {{ill|lt=younger Tachibanahime|Q11487396|WD=Q11487396|lt=younger Tachibanahime|1=Tachibanahime-no-Mikoto}}, commonly known as Yin-Yang Two Pillars (``Jingi Hoden'') {{Sfn|Kitabatake Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}} * {{ill|lt=Izanagi|Q813858|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagison|1=Izanagi}} Zainmine, {{ill|lt=Izanami|Q682306|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanagison|1=Izanami}}zainmine (“Hitachikuni 28 Shrines”) {{Sfn|Kitabatake Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}} * Yomine{{ill|lt=Hannyas|Q9285919|WD=Q9285919|lt=Haniyama Hikokami|1=Haniyasu-hiko and Haniyasu-hime}}, Inmine{{ill|lt=Hannyas|Q9285919|WD=Q9285919|lt=Haniyama Himekami|1=Haniyasu-hiko and Haniyasu-hime}} ("{{ill|lt=Divine Name Book Research|Q11588824|WD=Q11588824|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō Studies}}") {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}} * The enshrined deity is unknown, and legend says, ``Izanagison Zaiyomine, Izashoson Zainmine, commonly known as Tsukuba Daimyojin'' ({{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}'12 ({{ill|lt=1879|Q7783|WD=Q7783|1=1879}}) ``Mount Tsukuba Shrine Detailed Record'') {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}}After that, based on the records in the Six Kingdoms History, in January 1942 ({{ill|lt=1909|Q2057|WD=Q2057|1=1909}}), the names of the deities enshrined were determined to be ``Tsukuba Otokojin'' and ``Tsukuba Goddess.''{{Sfn|Meiji Shrine Magazine Materials|1912}}. Then, in {{ill|lt=Taisho|Q329174|WD=Q329174|1=Taishō era}}11 ({{ill|lt=1922|Q2165|WD=Q2165|1=1922}}), it was decided that ``Tsukuba Man God/Tsukuba Goddess'' should be written with ``Iza Nōson/Iza Shoson.''{{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}}. Furthermore, the origin and history of the tradition of Izaninoson and Izashozon is not clear. === History === === Founding === Founding date is unknown. Mount Tsukuba is said to have been revered since the time when people began living in the Kanto Plain, as it is so impressive that it is contrasted with {{ill|lt=Mt. Fuji|Q39231|WD=Q39231|1=Mount Fuji}} in the ``{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}''. According to the shrine biography (``Mt. Tsukuba Engi''), {{jalink|domestic production|Q3545163} written by Iza Nōson and Iza Shokuson in {{ill|lt=Kojiki|Q813031|WD=Q813031|1=Kojiki}}. }} "{{ill|lt=Onogoro Island|Q2985158|WD=Q2985158|lt=Onokoro Island|1=Onogoro Island}}" is said to correspond to Mt. Tsukuba {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. In addition, in "Shiririn Kayosho" ({{ill|lt=Nanbokucho Period (Japan)|Q264012|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho Period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}), Mt. Tsukuba is said to be the sacred mountain where {{ill|lt=Amaterasu Omikami|UNKNOWN|lt=Amaterasu Omikami}} descended. (era name)|Q1373146|Culture}} ({{ill|lt=1804|Q6894|WD=Q6894|1=1804}}-{{ill|lt=1818|Q6964|WD=Q6964|1=1818}}) "Kiji" also tells about the transfer of the same god from Tsukuba to Ise.Regarding the ritual clans, since Tsukuba no Mikoto (Tsukuba Mikoto, Tsukuba Mikoto), who appears in "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki", was appointed as the first {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Kunizo|Q11602846|WD=Q11602846|1=Tsukuba Kunizo}}, it is said that Tsukuba Kunizo served in unison with rituals and politicsThe founding tradition of the nearby {{ill|lt=Serikage Shrine|Q17228464|WD=Q17228464|1=Kokage Shrine}} (Kami-gun, Tsukuba City) also says that during the reign of {{ill|lt=Emperor Seimu|Q316672|WD=Q316672|1=Emperor Seimu}}, Tsukuba Kunizo's Akishiro-no-Mikoto enshrined Tsukuba Okami. . Many ancient tombs remain at the foot of Mt. Tsukuba, among which {{ill|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus (Tsukuba City)|Q17218702|WD=Q17218702|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus|1=Hachimanzuka-kofun}} (Numata, Tsukuba City) is thought to be a Tsukuba Kuni-zukuri tomb.{{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}}. The current main part of Tsukubasan Shrine is located around the worship hall, but the worship hall was built in 1875 on the site of Chuzenji Temple. Therefore, the "original Mt. Tsukuba Shrine" refers to the "Nantai Mt. Shrine and Nyotai Mt. Shrine". Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=412}}. . Also, although the date of its establishment is unknown, the ruins of Rokusho Shrine in Usui, Tsukuba City (currently a closed shrine) were the satomiya of both shrines (see section {{ill|lt=#Related locations|UNKNOWN|lt=Related locations}}). === Outline === ==== From the Nara period to the Heian period ==== ``{{ill|lt=Manyoshu|Q834321|WD=Q834321|1=Man'yōshū}}'' from the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|WD=Q189178|1=Nara period}} includes 25 poems from Tsukuba, and Mt. Tsukuba is said to have been the mountain representing {{ill|lt=Hitachi Province|Q1055353|WD=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}. Also, from the end of the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|WD=Q189178|1=Nara period}} to the beginning of the {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292|1=Heian period}}, the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hosso sect|1=UNKNOWN}} The monk {{ill|lt=Tokuichi|Q7813728|WD=Q7813728|1=Tokuitsu}} opened Tsukubasanji Temple, later Tsukubasan Chisokuin Chuzenji Temple {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. As a result, {{ill|lt=Shinto-Buddhist syncretism|Q2279088|WD=Q2279088|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and Mt. Tsukuba developed into one of the leading {{ill|lt=Shugendo|Q1483875|WD=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}} dojos {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} (for details, see the {{ill|lt=#Chuzenji|UNKNOWN|lt=Chuzenji}} section). During this period of syncretization of Shinto and Buddhism, it was also called ``Tsukuba Ryodaigongen'' (Ryobe Gongen).In the {{ill|lt=Rokukokushi|Q1151168|WD=Q1151168|lt=Kokushi|1=Rikkokushi}}, there is an article that says that in ancient times, in {{ill|lt=Honin|Q1373070|WD=Q1373070|1=Kōnin (era)}} 14 ({{ill|lt=823|Q29944|WD=Q29944|1=823}}) , the Tsukuba deity, which was lower than the Junior Fifth Rank, was made {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=government shrine|1=UNKNOWN}}. With the subsequent investiture of {{ill|lt=Divine Rank|Q11591025|WD=Q11591025|1=Shinkai (divine rank)}}, {{ill|lt=Jōkan (Japan)|Q1075635|WD=Q1075635|lt=Jōkan|1=Jōgan}}13 ({{ill|lt=871|Q24754|WD=Q24754|1=871}}), Tsukuba Ogami rose to Jusanmi (Junior Third Rank), and in Jogan 16 ({{ill|lt=874|Q23843|WD=Q23843|1=874}}) , Tsukuba Goddess rose to Jushini-Ji (or Sei-shii Shimi-ge <{{ill|lt=#Divine rank|UNKNOWN|lt=described later}}>).{{ill|lt=Extension (era name)|Q1327274|WD=Q1327274|lt=Extension|1=Enchō}} "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|WD=Q30470|1=927}}) Tsukuba District, Hitachi Province. In {{ill|lt=Hitachi-kuni|Q1055353|WD=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba-gun|Q7850092|WD=Q7850092|1=Tsukuba District, Ibaraki}} there are "Tsukubasan Shrine Niza Ichiza Meishindai It is listed as the only {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}} shrine in Tsukuba County, of which {{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}} is said to be the Tsukuba Man God, and the small shrine is said to be the Tsukuba Goddess {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. After that, in {{ill|lt=Jisho|Q1194671|WD=Q1194671|1=Jishō}} 4th year ({{ill|lt=1180|Q19702|WD=Q19702|1=1180}}), is said to have reached the rank of Shoichi. ==== From Kamakura period to Edo period ==== In the early {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, {{ill|lt=Tomoie Hatta|Q11391665|WD=Q11391665|1=Tomoie Hatta}} of {{ill|lt=Hitachi Province|Q1055353|WD=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Guo|Q1141023|WD=Q1141023|1=Shugo}} ({{ill|lt=Oda clan|Q11463150|WD=Q11463150|1=Oda clan}}'s son Hachiro Tameji inherited the name of Tsukuba Kunizo and became Tsukuba {{ill|lt=Betto|Q2900274|WD=Q2900274|1=Bettō}} {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The descendants of this Tameji Tsukuba (Myogen) thereafter called themselves the Tsukuba clan, and were the enshriners of the Tsukuba deity as well as the charge of Chuzenji temple {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The trends in the Middle Ages are not clear, but in {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185|1=Keichō}}5 ({{ill|lt=1600|Q6720|WD=Q6720|1=1600}}) Until the Tsukuba clan was removed by Kawaieyasu|Q171977}}, the Tsukuba deity, Chuzenji, is said to have been under the control of the Tsukuba clan {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, the {{ill|lt=Edo Shogunate|Q205662|WD=Q205662|lt=Bakufu|1=Tokugawa shogunate}} fiercely protected Chuzenji, many temples and pagodas were erected within the grounds of Chuzenji, and the character of Mt. Tsukuba changed from a co-existence of Shinto and Buddhism to a sacred place centered on Buddhism.{{Sfn|Mount Tsukuba Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Despite this patronage of Chuzen-ji Temple, the shadow of Tsukuba-kami was weak, and the form of Tsukuba-kami's enshrinement during this period is not clear {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (National History)|1988}} (for trends in the Edo period, see section {{ill|lt=#Chuzenji|UNKNOWN|lt=Chuzenji}}).At the end of the Edo period, the Tenguto raised an army in the first year of {{ill|lt=Genji|Q1325419|WD=Q1325419|1=Genji era}} ({{ill|lt=1864|Q7704|WD=Q7704|1=1864}}), and {{ja link|Tenguto Rebellion|Q1040831}} ({{ill|lt=Tenguto Rebellion#Mt.Tsukuba Raising of Arms|Q1040831|WD=Q1040831|lt=Mt. Tsukuba Incident|1=Mito Rebellion}}). ==== After Meiji ====

{{Harv|Kitabatake Tsukubayama Shrine|1984|p=414}}. === Precincts === The precincts of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine are 354 {{ill|lt=hectare|Q35852|WD=Q35852|1=Hectare}} on the south side of Mt. Tsukuba, more than 270 meters above sea level. . The main shrine is located on the summit of Mt. Nantai and Mt. Nyotai of Mt. Tsukuba, and there is a shrine on the mountainside where you can worship from a distance. === Tsukuba Yamanaka === [[File:Tsukubasan-jinja nantaisan-honden.JPG|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Nantaiyama Main Hall}}]] [[File:Mount Tsukuba Shrine on top.jpg|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Nyotaiyama Main Hall}}]] '''Mt. Nyotai Main Hall'' was built in {{ill|lt=Showa|Q327567|WD=Q327567|1=Shōwa era}}30 ({{ill|lt=1955|Q18577|WD=Q18577|1=1955}}), '''Mt. The main hall''' was renovated in 1979 ({{ill|lt=1979|Q2484|WD=Q2484|1=1979}}), and both are Ikkensha {{ill|lt=Ryuzo|Q210684|WD=Q210684|1=Nagare-zukuri}}. At the summit of Mt. Nantai, there is a joint observatory with {{ill|lt=University of Tsukuba|Q743615|WD=Q743615|1=University of Tsukuba}} {{ill|lt=Joint Meteorological Observatory of Tsukubasan Shrine and University of Tsukuba Computational Science Research Center|Q11602877|WD=Q11602877|1=Meteorological Station of the Mt. Tsukuba Shrine & Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba}} (facilities and land owned by Tsukubasan Shrine Hayashi (2007): p. 7. Nishimura (2010): p. 559. ) At the summit of Mt. Nyotai, there is a shrine awarding place and Ama no Ukihashi (rebuilt in April 2009). The saddle between the two peaks is called ``Miyukigahara.'' About 300 meters to Mt. Nantai and about 600 meters to Mt. Nyotai. The Tsukuba Cable Car's Tsukuba Sancho Station is located here, and there are many souvenir shops and restaurants.In addition, in the mountains there is also the "Men and Women River," which is famous as the subject of {{ill|lt=Emperor Yozei|Q349280|WD=Q349280|lt=Yoseiin|1=Emperor Yōzei}}'s poem {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ogura Hyakunin Isshu|1=UNKNOWN}}. (Ibaraki Prefecture) In addition to the source of the Minanogawa River, there is also the Shihosugi Cedar. There are many sacred stones, strangely shaped rocks, and famous trees, such as the {{ill|lt=cedar|Q147388|WD=Q147388|1=Cryptomeria}} named ``Cedar'' (near the headwaters of the Men and Women River), which is estimated to be 800 years old, ``Benkei Seven Returns'', ``Mother's Womb Passing'', and ``Gama Stone''. These rocky areas were once used as a dojo for {{ill|lt=Shugendo|Q1483875|WD=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}}, and Mt. Tsukuba meditation is still performed as a Shinto ritual. === Around the shrine === [[File:Tsukubasan-jinja zuishinmon.JPG|thumb|160px|right|{{Center|Zuishinmon
(Tsukuba City designated cultural property)}}]] [[File:Tsukubasan Shrine Oshinbashi Front.JPG|thumb|160px|right|{{Center|Shinbashi
(Ibaraki Prefecture Designated Cultural Property)}}]] A {{ill|lt=monzen town|Q10564515|WD=Q10564515|1=Monzen-machi}} is formed around the worship hall, which forms the main part of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. However, before the Meiji era, this area was a sacred place centered on Buddhism, with Chuzenji as its main temple {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}, but when Chuzenji was abolished after the Meiji Restoration, it was revived as a shrine and a worship hall was built.``The Hall of Worship'' was built in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}8 ({{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|WD=Q7764|1=1875}}). The plaque on the front, "Tsukuba Shrine," is written by {{ill|lt=Prince Komatsunomiya Akihito|Q712627|WD=Q712627|1=Prince Komatsu Akihito}} and engraved by {{ill|lt=Koun Takamura|Q2080344|WD=Q2080344|1=Takamura Kōun}} from Famous Places Guide (Mito Transportation Office, 1927), page 3. . Before the Meiji period, there was the main hall (Omido) of Chuzenji Temple at this location, but after the Omido was abolished due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, a new one was built {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The foundation stone remains in front of the worship hall, reminiscent of the Chuzenji temple {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubasan Shrine|1984|p=418}}. Furthermore, Omido has been rebuilt as {{ill|lt=Omido (Tsukuba City)|Q11435427|WD=Q11435427|lt=Omido|1=Ōmi-dō}} of the {{ill|lt=Toyoyama School of Shingon Sect|Q3077351|WD=Q3077351|1=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha}} Omido Church to the southwest of the worship hall.The ``Zuishinmon'' (Zuishinmon) built in front of the worship hall is a tower gate with a width of 5 x 2 shaku and a depth of 3 x 3, making it one of the largest in Ibaraki Prefecture. . It was originally donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in {{ill|lt=Kanei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913|1=Kan'ei}}10 ({{ill|lt=1633|Q6870|WD=Q6870|1=1633}}), but {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Horeki|1=UNKNOWN}} It was burnt down in 4th year ({{ill|lt=1754|Q7623|WD=Q7623|1=1754}}), and although it was rebuilt, it was burnt down again in 4th year of Meiwa ({{ill|lt=1767|Q7672|WD=Q7672|1=1767}}). The current tower gate was rebuilt in {{ill|lt=Bunka (era name)|Q1373146|WD=Q1373146|lt=Bunka|1=Bunka}}8 ({{ill|lt=1811|Q6928|WD=Q6928|1=1811}}). During the {{ill|lt=syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism|Q2279088|WD=Q2279088|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} period, Nio statues (Vajra Rikishi statues) were enshrined there as ``Niomon'', but after {{ill|lt=Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|Q1970535|WD=Q1970535|1=Shinbutsu bunri}}, it was called ``Zuishinmon''. During the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, the Nio statue was floated down the Sakuragawa River on a raft and taken to Tofukuji Temple in Matsuzuka, Tsukuba City. For this reason, it is now called ``Nagare Nio.'' Takayoshi Nishitani. The sacred mountain of Mt. Tsukuba and Tokuichi Daishi: Chisoku-in Chuzenji and Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. Ibaraki Prefecture Local Culture Honor Society, 2012. At the current Zuishinmon gate, the Zuishin statue of {{ill|lt=Yamato Takeru|Q461258|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}} (Yamato Takeru no Mikoto) is enshrined on the left side of the shrine, and on the right side is the Zuishin statue of {{ill|lt=Yamato Takeru|Q461258|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}}. This Zuishinmon gate has been designated as a cultural property designated by Tsukuba City.Beside the Zuishinmon gate is the Koyo Shonin Five Ring Tower. This is the only temple-related {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=doto pagoda|1=UNKNOWN}} that remains at Tsukubasan Shrine, which was spared from destruction and relocation during {{ill|lt=Haitbutsu Kishaku|Q702298|WD=Q702298|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} in the early Meiji period. One theory is that Kotan was the son of {{ill|lt=Hidetada Tokugawa|Q314464|WD=Q314464|1=Tokugawa Hidetada}}'s wet nurse, and entered the Betsto Chisoku-in temple on Mt. Tsukuba in 1611. {{ill|lt=Osaka no Siege|Q475780|WD=Q475780|lt=Osaka Summer Siege and Winter Siege|1=Siege of Osaka}} He is said to have served in the army and prayed for victory, and is said to have died on December 19, 1624, {{ill|lt=Kanei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913|1=Kan'ei}}{{Cite book|Japanese book|title=Kanto's Famous Mountain, Mt. Tsukuba, Guide to Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|publisher=Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|year=2008|page=40}}.The ``Shinkyo Bridge'' built on the approach is {{ill|lt=Gabled|Q13308575|WD=Q13308575|1=Kirizuma-style}} with a thatched roof, 1 ken in frontage and 4 ken in depth, and is a sled bridge in the {{ill|lt=Azuchi-Momoyama period|Q319531|WD=Q319531|1=Azuchi–Momoyama period}} style. {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Shinbashi}}. It is said to have been donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1633, and was renovated by the fifth shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi|Q313745|WD=Q313745|1=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi}} in {{ill|lt=Genroku|Q1325001|WD=Q1325001|1=Genroku}}15 ({{ill|lt=1702|Q6819|WD=Q6819|1=1702}}). During the Spring and Autumn Gozachange Festival, mikoshi and attendants cross here {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Shinbashi}}. Worshipers are normally prohibited from crossing the bridge, and are only allowed during the Spring and Autumn Gozagae Festival and the February Toshikoshi Festival . This Shinbashi bridge is designated as a cultural property of Ibaraki Prefecture. A bronze statue of {{ill|lt=Koshiro Fujita|Q11288247|WD=Q11288247|1=Fujita Kishirō}} is erected near the entrance to the shrine. Koshiro Fujita was the fourth son of {{ill|lt=Toko Fujita|Q6564466|WD=Q6564466|1=Fujita Tōko}} and was the leader of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tenguto|1=UNKNOWN}} Tsukuba faction that raised an army at Mt. Tsukuba on March 27, 1864 (May 2, 1864). A plaque by Mito local historians Ohsui Ando and Saburo Yumene was installed near the statue in 1990.Additionally, Kasuga Shrine, Hie Shrine, and Itsukushima Shrine, which were built as guardian shrines of Chuzenji Temple, remain today as the final shrines of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (see section {{ill|lt=#terminal shrine|UNKNOWN|lt=terminal shrine}}). Near Kasuga Hie Shrine stands a variety of camphor tree {{ill|lt=Marubagus|Q24868661|WD=Q24868661|1=Cinnamomum camphora var. rotundifolia}} (Marubagusu), which is designated as a natural monument by Tsukuba City, and near the tower gate stands a large cedar tree that is about 800 years old and 32 meters tall. In addition, within the precincts are the grave of {{ill|lt=Masakatsu Kusunoki|Q11541195|WD=Q11541195|1=Kusunoki Masakatsu}}, the grandson of {{ill|lt=Masashige Kusunoki|Q382234|WD=Q382234|1=Kusunoki Masashige}}, and the space egg that was exhibited at the {{ill|lt=International Science and Technology Exposition|Q2312924|WD=Q2312924|1=Expo 85 (Tsukuba, Japan)}} (Science Expo). Although normally closed to the public, there is also a storehouse that collects various materials provided to pray for and express gratitude for the success of each pavilion (it was opened to the public for a limited time in July 2006). Additionally, monuments of 25 Tsukuba poems from the Manyoshu have been erected around Mt. Tsukuba, including Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. Both shrines are enshrined along the Hakuunbashi course in Mt. Tsukuba, and enshrine the {{ill|lt=mikogami|Q352176|WD=Q352176|1=Mikogami}} ({{ill|lt=Mikiko|Q4702904|WD=Q4702904|1=Three Noble Children}} and Ebisu no Mikoto) of Izanagison and Izashoson. * Inamura Shrine ({{Coord|36|13|27.5|N|140|6|41.6|E|region:JP-08|name=Inamura Shrine}}) *:* Deity enshrined: {{ill|lt=Amaterasu Omikami|Q455602|WD=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Omikami|1=Amaterasu}} (Amaterasu Omikami) *: It is enshrined on a huge stone at the end of Benkei Seven Return. This megalith is also called "{{ill|lt=Takamagahara|Q1141974|WD=Q1141974|1=Takamagahara}}". * Azatsune Shrine ({{Coord|36|13|28.5|N|140|6|26|E|region:JP-08|name=Azatsune Shrine}}) *:* Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Susanoo|Q272993|WD=Q272993|lt=Susanoo|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} (Susanoo no Mikoto) *: Enshrined in front of ``Byobu Rock'' beyond ``Hokuto Rock''. * Koharagi Shrine ({{Coord|36|13|30.3|N|140|6|31.8|E|region:JP-08|name=Obaraki Shrine}}) *:* Enshrined deity: {{ill|WD=Q595520|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|WD=Q595520|WD=Q595520|lt=Tsukuyomi no Mikoto|1=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto}} *: Enshrined under "Hokuto Rock" (based on the legend that {{ill|lt=Kukai|Q222227|WD=Q222227|lt=Kobo Daishi|1=Kūkai}} saw {{ill|lt=Myoken Bodhisattva|Q10960623|WD=Q10960623|1=Myōken}}).* Watari Shrine ({{Coord|36|13|29.8|N|140|6|36.6|E|region:JP-08|name=Watari Shrine}}) *:* Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Hiruko|Q1067028|WD=Q1067028|lt=Ebisu no Mikoto|1=Hiruko}} (Hiruko no Mikoto) *: Enshrined near the strange rock "Uramen Daikoku". In addition, at the former Rokusho Shrine (Usui, Tsukuba City: Tsukubasan Shrine Motosato Shrine) and Rokusho Shrine (Izumi, Tsukuba City), the ``Rokusho'', which includes the above-mentioned four sessha shrines, was enshrined in addition to the two deities of Tsukuba Men and Women. Most of them are still located in the mountains, and the following six shrines are located around the shrine. * Hie Shrine/Kasuga Shrine ** Hie Shrine enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Oyama Kuijin|Q10935105|WD=Q10935105|1=Oyamakui no Kami}} ** Deities enshrined at Kasuga Shrine: {{ill|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|WD=Q1502690|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi-kami|1=Takemikazuchi}}, {{ill|lt=Tunetsu-nushi-kami|Q1107286|WD=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi}}, {{ill|lt=Amagiya-no-Mikoto|Q2564508|WD=Q2564508|lt=Amenoyane-kami|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}, {{ill|lt=Hime-kami|Q22070227|WD=Q22070227|1=Himegami}} *: Both shrines are located adjacent to the left side of the main hall of worship, and share the hall of worship. To the east is Hie Shrine, and to the west is Kasuga Shrine. The enshrined deity is said to have been enshrined as a guardian shrine at the time of the founding of Chuzenji Temple. Both the main shrine and the worship hall are said to have been donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1633 (1633).*: The main shrine is a three-way shrine {{ill|lt=Nagazuzukuri|Q210684|WD=Q210684|1=Nagare-zukuri}} that has the same size and structure, and has a width of 2 rooms and a depth of 2 rooms.Hie Shrine and Kasuga Shrine information boards. . On the toad in the center of the back, a monkey is carved at Hie Shrine and a deer is carved at Kasuga Shrine.{{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Kasuga Shrine Hie Shrine}}. The worship hall is in the Warihaiden style, with 5 ken rows and 2 beams {{ill|lt=Irimoya-zukuri|Q855025|WD=Q855025|1=East Asian hip-and-gable roof}}, with eaves and gables on the front and back . The main shrine and worship hall of both shrines have been designated as Ibaraki Prefecture's designated cultural properties. * Itsukushima Shrine ** Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Ichikishima Hime|Q11059454|WD=Q11059454|lt=Ichikishima Hime no Mikoto|1=Ichikishima-hime}} *: Enshrined in the pond southwest of the main hall of worship. The enshrined deity is , which is said to be Kansei from {{ill|lt=Lake Biwa|Q200239|WD=Q200239|1=Lake Biwa}}{{ill|lt=Chikubushima|Q2975401|WD=Q2975401|1=Chikubu Island}}. The shrine building is said to have been donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1633. {{ill|lt=Kasugazukuri|Q3193781|WD=Q3193781|1=Kasuga-zukuri}}Itsukushima Shrine information board with a frontage of 1.5 rooms and a depth of 10 feet. . A serpent divine messenger is carved on the front of the shrine.{{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Itsukushima Shrine Main Hall}}. This shrine building has been designated as a cultural property by Ibaraki Prefecture. * Asahi Inari Shrine ** Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Ota Mikoto|Q97496337|WD=Q97496337|1=Ōta-no-Mikoto}}*: Another name is ``Shusse Inari.'' It is located behind the main hall of worship. It is said to have been founded by {{ill|lt=Emperor Saga|Q316654|WD=Q316654|1=Emperor Saga}}, the fourth prince of Hitachi Province, {{ill|lt=Imperial Prince Tadayoshi|Q17210943|WD=Q17210943|1=Tadayoshi-shinnō}}. * Inari Shrine (Inari Shrine) *: It is located next to Asahi Inari Shrine. * Atago Shrine (Atagoyama Shrine) *: Enshrined at the back of the east side of the main hall of worship. (Ibaraki Prefecture designated cultural property) === Approach === The ancient approach to the shrine is known as ``''{{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefectural Road No. 139 Tsukubayama Park Line|Q11617553|WD=Q11617553|lt=Tsukuba Road|1=Ibaraki Prefectural Road Route 139}}'''. The road starting from Hojo, Tsukuba City and leading to the shrine ({{Google Map Route Map 2 |1=36.17782412531196,140.09265904155927|2=36.213667,+140.101306|3=@36.2112566,140.0984105,17z|data=!4m10!4m9!1m3!2m 2!1d140.092659!2d36.1778241!1m3!2m2!1d140.101306!2d36.213667!3e2?hl}}), and is currently followed by {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefectural Route 139 Tsukubayama Park Line|Q11617553|WD=Q11617553|1=Ibaraki Prefectural Road Route 139}}. The entire section has been selected as one of {{ill|lt=Japan's top 100 roads|Q11506119|WD=Q11506119|1=100 Best Roads in Japan}}. Also, on the way to the shrine, there is a torii gate at 6-chome. This torii gate was built in {{ill|lt=Horeki|Q1194397|WD=Q1194397|1=Hōreki}}9 ({{ill|lt=1759|Q7643|WD=Q7643|1=1759}}), and it is said that it used to have a plaque that read "Tsukuba Shrine, the Creation of Heaven and Earth". . During the Spring and Autumn Gozagae Festival, there is a shrine ceremony from the worship hall to this point.On the other hand, the current main route is {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefectural Route 42 Kasama Tsukuba Line|Q11617758|WD=Q11617758|1=Ibaraki Prefectural Road Route 42}} from {{ill|lt=Kanto Railway Tsukuba Kita Office|Q11602873|WD=Q11602873|lt=Tsukuba Yamaguchi Bus Terminal|1=Tsukuba Yamaguchi Bus Terminal}}. In the past, the {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Station|Q18575588|WD=Q18575588|1=Tsukuba Station}} of the {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Railway Tsukuba Line|Q11602898|WD=Q11602898|1=Tsukuba Line}} was also located at the same bus terminal, and a large torii gate has been built near the station site. In addition, {{ill|lt=cattail oil|Q11296148|WD=Q11296148|1=Gama-abura}} ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=ointment|1=UNKNOWN}}) is known as a specialty of the approach. The story of the cattail oil seller has been certified as a local intangible folk cultural property by Tsukuba City, and preservation efforts are underway. In ancient times, it was held on the winter and summer solstice, and it is said that the gods of summer and winter take turns in the divine seat {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (official website) | Annual event}}. The festival consists of the following three festivals. * Kanmisosai *: Changing the clothes of the god at the main shrine at the summit {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (official website)|annual event}}. * Hobeisai *: Dedicating a coin to the shrine {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (official website)|annual event}}. *Jinkousai *: During the Kami Festival, the Kami clothing removed from the previous season is placed in a mikoshi, and the shrine parishioners {{ill|lt=passing|Q11561919|WD=Q11561919|1=passing}} {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (official website)|annual event}}. On both days of this festival, you will be allowed to cross the Shinbashi Bridge, a cultural property designated by Ibaraki Prefecture. In addition, the current Shinko Festival is a journey to the first torii gate, but before 1910, it was a journey to Rokusho Shrine (currently closed) in Satomiya {{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. There are many examples of the gods being alternated between the village shrine and the mountain shrine, and it is said that prayers for fertility are based on the alternation of the rice god and the mountain god {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubayama Shrine|1984|p=419}}. === Cultural assets === === Important cultural property (designated by the country) === * Tachi Meiyoshiso (with attached Itomaki Tachi Koshirae) (craft) *: {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, sword made by Yoshimune, a swordsmith of the Bizen Ichimonji school {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Yoshimune}}. However, there are multiple people with the name Yoshimune in the Bizen Ichimonji school, and it is not certain which one was the author of this work {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Yoshimune}}. This sword was donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in {{ill|lt=Kanei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913|1=Kan'ei}} 10 ({{ill|lt=1633|Q6870|WD=Q6870|1=1633}}) when the temple and pagoda of Chuzenji Temple on Mt. Tsukuba were being rebuilt.{{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Yoshimune}}. The Tachi Koshirae has Aoi crests inlaid on the metal fittings of the handle and scabbard {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Yoshimune}}. Tsukuba is written. === Chuzenji === '''Chuzenji'' (Chuzenji) is a Muhonji temple {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} of the {{ill|lt=Shingon sect|Q550182|WD=Q550182|1=Shingon Buddhism}} that existed in the area centered around the worship hall of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. {{ill|lt=Mountain name|Q11058522|WD=Q11058522|1=sangō}} is Mt. Tsukuba, and the temple name is Chisoku-in. The principal image is {{ill|lt=Senju Kannon|Q10904910|WD=Q10904910|1=Thousand-armed Kannon}}. It was also the 25th temple of {{ill|lt=Bando Thirty-Three Kannon|Q806417|WD=Q806417|1=Bandō Sanjūsankasho}} {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. It is said to have started with {{ill|lt=Tokuichi|Q7813728|WD=Q7813728|1=Tokuitsu}}, a monk of the {{ill|lt=Hosso sect|Q349849|WD=Q349849|1=East Asian Yogācāra}}, who opened ``Tsukubasan-dera''. is also found in "{{ill|lt=Genkoshasho|Q4153225|WD=Q4153225|1=Genkō Shakusho}}" of {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}} {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Its founding year is the first year of {{ill|lt=Enryaku|Q1373176|WD=Q1373176|1=Enryaku}} ({{ill|lt=782 years|Q30550|WD=Q30550|1=782}}) , Enryaku era (782-{{ill|lt=806|Q30021|WD=Q30021|1=806}}) {{Sfn|Chuzenji ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}, {{ill|lt=Tencho|Q1373138|WD=Q1373138|1=Tenchō}} first year ({{ill|lt=824|Q30353|WD=Q30353|1=824}}) {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba-san Shrine|1984|p=416}}, Tencho era (824-{{ill|lt=834|Q30381|WD=Q30381|1=834}}) {{Sfn|Tsukubasan-jinja Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}, etc.With the opening of Tsukuba-san Temple, the two deities of Mt. Tsukuba, male and female, came to be enshrined as ``Mt. Tsukuba Ryobu Gongen,'' with Kannon as the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=real Buddha|1=UNKNOWN}} {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Since Mt. Tsukuba has been a place for mountain training since ancient times, temples gradually flourished after that, and the name of the temple is said to have come to be called Chuzen-ji ('''Mt. Tsukuba Chisoku-in Chuzen-ji'') {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. {{ill|lt=Middle Ages|Q12554|WD=Q12554|1=Middle Ages}} include Mt. Nikko ({{ill|lt=Rinnoji|Q1348249|WD=Q1348249|1=Rinnō-ji}}), Mt. Sagami Daisen ({{ill|lt=Oyama Afuri Shrine|Q11434713|WD=Q11434713|lt=Daisenji|1=Ōyama Afuri Shrine}}), and Izu Hasashiyu ({{jal Ink|Izusan Shrine|Q611460|Izusan Sansho Gongen}}), {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} is said to have been one of the leading {{ill|lt=Shugendo|Q1483875|WD=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}} sacred sites in the Kanto region. The charge was held by the Tsukuba clan, starting with Tameji Tsukuba (Myogen) {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}.The situation in the Middle Ages is not known, but in the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it was protected by the shogunate as a place of prayer for {{ill|lt=Kimon|Q11673539|WD=Q11673539|1=Kimon}}, and the temple flourished again {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|WD=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} abolished the Tsukuba clan from the Tsukuba mountain betto in {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185|1=Keichō}} 5th year ({{ill|lt=1600|Q6720|WD=Q6720|1=1600}}), appointed Yutoshi as the founder of the Chukyo era, and established the Keicho era. In 1602|Q6727}}, he donated 500 koku as a divine territory, and in 15 Keicho years ({{ill|lt=1610|Q6765|WD=Q6765|1=1610}}), he donated 500 koku as a temple territory. In addition, the third shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|Q314481|WD=Q314481|1=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} restored the two shrines on the mountaintop, and also built the main hall (Omido), three-storied pagoda, bell tower, tower gate, Shinkyo Bridge, and shrines within the precincts of Hie, Kasuga, and Itsukushima {{Sfn|Ruins of Chuzenji Temple (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Also, during the time of the fifth shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi|Q313745|WD=Q313745|1=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi}}, it was renamed ``''Gojiin'''', and the temple territory counted 1,500 koku {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. After that, it continued to develop as a sacred mountain throughout the Edo period, and the {{ill|lt=monzen town|Q10564515|WD=Q10564515|1=Monzen-machi}} also developed {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}.After the Meiji Restoration, due to the {{ill|lt=Haibutsu Kishaku|Q702298|WD=Q702298|1=Haibutsu kishaku}}, the functions of Chuzenji ceased, the halls and pagodas were destroyed except for some shrine buildings, and the ritual implements were scattered all over the place {{Sfn|Ruins of Chuzenji Temple (Heibonsha)|1982}}. In 1930 (1930|Q18787}}), '''{{ill|lt=Omido (Tsukuba City)|Q11435427|WD=Q11435427|lt=Omido|1=Ōmi-dō}}''' (Omido) was rebuilt as a temple of the {{ill|lt=Shingon sect Toyozan school|Q3077351|WD=Q3077351|1=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha}} to the southwest of the worship hall of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine, and it continues to this day. === Related locations === [[File:Rokusho-jinja Ruins (Tsukuba) keidai.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Ruins of Rokusho Shrine (Usui, Tsukuba City)}}{{Small|Satomiya ruins of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. }}]] [[File:Hachimanzuka-kofun (Tsukuba) zenkei.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|[[Hachimanzuka Tumulus (Tsukuba City)|Hachimanzuka Tumulus]] (Numata, Tsukuba City)}}]] === Ruins of Rokusho Shrine === : Located in Tsukuba City {{ill|lt=Usui (Tsukuba City)|Q17194126|WD=Q17194126|lt=Usui|1=Usui, Tsukuba}} ({{Coord|36|12|2.18|N|140|6|38.53|E|region:JP-08|name=Motosato Shrine Ruins of Rokusho Shrine}}). : Also known as ``Rokusho Kodaijingu Ruins.'' The site of Satomiya, now a closed shrine. ``Rokusho'' is a general term for the two shrines of Tsukuba's male and female gods and the four shrines of Setsusha {{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. It is said that in the past, there were two shrines dedicated to the male and female deities, a worship hall, a Zuishinmon gate, and a treasure trove.{{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} This Rokusho Shrine was closed in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}43 ({{ill|lt=1910|Q2075|WD=Q2075|1=1910}}), and the divine spirit was (Tsukuba City)|Q17209343|Kamigun}} It was enshrined in the {{ill|lt=Kakekage Shrine|Q17228464|WD=Q17228464|1=Kokage Shrine}} (Kakekageyama Shrine) in the {{Sfn|Rokusho Shrine Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. : According to "Silk Shadow Mountain Shintokuki", in the 20th year of {{ill|lt=Enryaku|Q1373176|WD=Q1373176|1=Enryaku}} ({{ill|lt=801|Q30008|WD=Q30008|1=801}}), k|Sakanoue Tamuramaro|Q941979}} is said to have deposited horse harnesses, a treasured sword, and a divine mirror here on his way back from the Ezo conquest. {{Sfn|Ruins of Rokusho Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. When the torii gate collapsed in the 3rd year of the Meiji era ({{ill|lt=1870|Q7741|WD=Q7741|1=1870}}), a bronze mirror was unearthed, and it is said that there was an inscription on the mirror that read, ``Stone torii gate, Seii Taishogun Sakanoue Tamuramaro erected'' {{Sfn|Ruins of Rokusho Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. === {{ill|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus (Tsukuba City)|Q17218702|WD=Q17218702|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus|1=Hachimanzuka-kofun}} === : Located in Numata, Tsukuba City ({{Coord|36|12|23.54|N|140|4|41.24|E|region:JP-08|name=Hachimanzuka Tumulus}}). : Located at the southwest foot of Mt. Tsukuba, this is the largest {{ill|lt=kofun|Q1141225|WD=Q1141225|1=Kofun}} in the Tsukuba region. This is a {{ill|lt=keyhole-shaped tumulus|Q11268718|WD=Q11268718|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} with a length of 90 meters, and is thought to have been constructed in the first half of the {{ill|lt=6th century|Q8090|WD=Q8090|1=6th century}}. . Abeshiko no Mikoto of the first generation {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Kunizo|Q11602846|WD=Q11602846|1=Tsukuba Kunizo}}About Tsukuba Kunizo, "{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" In Tsukuba Gunjo, Tsukuba no Mikoto (Tsukuba Mikoto) was the reign of the 10th {{ill|lt=Emperor Sujin|Q333530|WD=Q333530|1=Emperor Sujin}}. He was dispatched to ``{{ill|lt=Sendai Kūjihonki|Q2716751|WD=Q2716751|1=Kujiki}}'' ``Kokuzohonki'' In Tsukuba Kunizojo, Akoshiiro no Mikoto, the grandson of Ninko Takami no Mikoto, was appointed as the successor of the 13th Emperor, {{ill|lt=Emperor Seimu|Q316672|WD=Q316672|1=Emperor Seimu}}. Regarding this, there is a theory that the genealogy goes as ``Oshinobu no Mikoto - Chikutan no Mikoto - Akuseiro no Mikoto'', and another theory that Chikutan no Mikoto was a pioneer and the first generation was Akuseiro no Mikoto {{Harv|Tsukuba Province (Kadokawa)|1983}}. It is said to be the tomb of Mt. Tsukuba, and its relationship with the rituals of Mt. Tsukuba has been pointed out {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubasan Shrine|1984|p=414}}. There are many other ancient tombs in addition to this one, located at the southern foot of Mt. Tsukuba.{{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Yawatazuka}} === Local information === ; Location * Hall of worship/office: {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|WD=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba City|Q273863|WD=Q273863|1=Tsukuba}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba (Tsukuba City)|Q11602837|WD=Q11602837|lt=Tsukuba|1=Tsukuba}}1 ; Transportation access * bus ** {{ill|lt=Tokyo New Urban Railway Tsukuba Express|Q1377699|WD=Q1377699|lt=Tsukuba Express|1=Tsukuba Express}} From {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Station|Q1069714|WD=Q1069714|1=Tsukuba Station}} ({{ill|lt=Tsukuba Center|Q11272231|WD=Q11272231|1=Tsukuba Center}}), take the Mt. Tsukuba (direct) {{ill|lt=shuttle bus|Q1368498|WD=Q1368498|1=Shuttle bus}} and get off at the "Mt. Tsukuba Shrine Iriguchi" bus stop. (About 40 minutes on board, 10 minutes walk after getting off) ** From the {{ill|lt=Kanto Railway Tsukuba Kita Office|Q11602873|WD=Q11602873|lt=Tsukuba Yamaguchi Bus Terminal|1=Tsukuba Yamaguchi Bus Terminal}} at the foot of the mountain, take the {{ill|lt=Kanto Railway #Bus Business|Q845943|WD=Q845943|lt=Kanto Railway Bus|1=Kantō Railway}} and get off at the "Tsukubasan Jinja Iriguchi" bus stop (about 15 minutes on board, about 10 minutes' walk after getting off) * car ** Parking lots cost around 500 yen for direct, public, and private parking lots. However, you can use the paid parking lot at Tsukubasanjinja Shrine for free for one hour. . The farthest Tsukuba Municipal Parking Lot No. 1 is open for free (except during the Mt. Tsukuba plum grove season), but it requires a long walk along a busy prefectural road.For information on climbing to the main shrine of Mt. Nantai and Mt. Nyotai, see "{{ill|lt=Mt. Tsukuba #climbing|Q1754619|WD=Q1754619|1=Mount Tsukuba}}". Nyotai, and the large torii gate can be seen on the mountainside. }}]] [[File:Tsukubasan-jinja ōtorii.JPG|thumb|right|200px|{{Center|Ōtorii}}]]'''Tsukubasan Shrine'' (Tsukubasan Shrine) is located in {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|WD=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba City|Q273863|WD=Q273863|1=Tsukuba}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba (Tsukuba City)|Q11602837|WD=Q11602837|lt=Tsukuba|1=Tsukuba}}. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinai Shrine|1=Shikinaisha|WD=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}} 1 shrine, 1 small shrine). {{ill|lt=Modern shrine rank system|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Old shrine rank|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=prefectural shrine|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}, and currently it is {{ill|lt=Beppon Shrine|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of {{ill|lt=Shrine Headquarters|Q908077|WD=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. === Overview === It is a shrine that enshrines {{ill|lt=Mt. Tsukuba|Q1754619|WD=Q1754619|1=Mount Tsukuba}}, which rises to the southwest of {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|WD=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}} in the northeastern part of the {{ill|lt=Kanto Plain|Q1124865|WD=Q1124865|1=Kantō Plain}}, as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}}, and the main shrine buildings are located in the following three locations. :* '''Mt. Nantai Main Hall'' - The summit of the west peak (Mt. Nantai, 871 meters above sea level). :* '''Mt. Nyotai Main Hall''' - The summit of the eastern peak (Mt. Nyotai, 877 meters above sea level.The elevation of Mt. Nyotai was revised from 876 meters in 1999.). :* '''Hotel'''' - Mountainside (270 meters above sea level). View both main shrines from a distance. Mt. Tsukuba is a double-eared peak consisting of a west peak and an east peak, and the main shrine of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine is located on each peak. The precincts are vast, with the shrine site extending over the 270 meter above sea level line (prayer hall) on the south side of Mt. Tsukuba, and its area is approximately 354 {{ill|lt=ha|Q35852|WD=Q35852|1=Hectare}}. A {{ill|lt=monzen town|Q10564515|WD=Q10564515|1=Monzen-machi}} is formed around the worship hall halfway up the south side. Generally speaking, ``Tsukubasan Shrine'' often refers to the area around this worship hall. To the west of the shrine is Miyawaki Station of {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Scenic Railway|Q11602894|WD=Q11602894|1=Tsukuba Scenic Railway}}'s {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Scenic Railway Tsukuba Cable Railway Line|Q6924212|WD=Q6924212|lt=Mt. Tsukuba Cable Car|1=Mount Tsukuba Cable Car}}, and there is also a trailhead, which is crowded with not only worshipers but also mountain climbers.Mt. Tsukuba has been deeply worshiped as a divine mountain ever since it appeared in ``{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}},'' and Mt. Tsukuba Shrine, which enshrines the divine spirit, was deeply revered by court nobles and samurai families. As for cultural properties, the long sword (Mei Yoshimune) has been designated as a national {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Property|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}, and several shrine buildings have been designated as tangible cultural properties by Ibaraki Prefecture and Tsukuba City. === Enshrined God === The main {{ill|lt=enshrined deity|Q11591100|WD=Q11591100|1=Saijin}} is the following two pillars: :* '''Tsukuba Otoko no Kami'' (Tsukuba Otokami, Tsukuba Otokami) :*: The god of Mt. Nantai. The personal god is '''{{ill|lt=Izanagi|Q813858|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi no Mikoto|1=Izanagi}}''' (Izanagi no Mikoto). :* '''Tsukuba Goddess''' (Tsukuba Goddess) :*: God of Mount Nyotai. The personal god is '''{{ill|lt=Izanami|Q682306|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami no Mikoto|1=Izanami}}'''. The {{ill|lt=Shintai|Q327532|WD=Q327532|1=Shintai}} of the main shrine is a divine robe (kanmiso), which is replaced at the Gozakae Festival {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Official Website)|Tsukubasan Shrine History}}. In addition, in "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Meiji Shrine Journals|1=UNKNOWN}}" it is referred to as a divine mirror {{Sfn|Meiji Shrine Journals|1912}}. Since the two gods Izanago no Mikoto and Iza Shokuson got married and gave birth to many gods and domestic births, they are believed to have blessings such as matchmaking, marital harmony, family safety, child-bearing, and child rearing. It is also said to have blessings such as traffic safety and construction safety. === About the enshrined deity === Mt. Tsukuba is a double-eared peak consisting of Mt. Nantai and Mt. Nyotai, each of which is dedicated to a deity. It is said that because of the mountain's appearance, with its two peaks side by side, it was natural for two male and female ancestor deities to be enshrined here. "{{ill|lt=Hitachi Province Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" "Hitachi Province Fudoki" Tsukuba-gunjo (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). Regarding Mt. Tsukuba, writes that the west peak (Mt. Nantai) was so steep that climbing it was prohibited as it was considered a divine peak. On the other hand, Higashimine (Mt. Nyotai) is steep, but springs flow constantly in summer and winter, and it is said that men and women gathered there in spring and autumn to perform {{ill|lt=utagaki|Q610915|WD=Q610915|1=Utagaki}}. In this way, Mt. Nantai was considered a restricted area, while Mt. Nyotai was considered an open area, and at the time the Fudoki was compiled, their characteristics were already very different. Numerous ritual artifacts have also been discovered near Mt. Nyotai from the end of the 7th century to the 12th century {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba (Kadokawa)|1983}}. The name of the god is written in {{ill|lt=Rokukokushi|Q1151168|WD=Q1151168|1=Rikkokushi}} as ``Tsukuba male god'' and ``Tsukuba goddess.'' In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, there were some theories that posited a personal god, and the following description can be found in the literature:{{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubasan Shrine|1984|p=414}}* Ichishasha {{ill|lt=Yamato Takeru|Q461258|WD=Q461258|lt=Nihon Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, Ichishasha {{ill|lt=younger Tachibanahime|Q11487396|WD=Q11487396|lt=younger Tachibanahime|1=Tachibanahime-no-Mikoto}}, commonly known as Yin-Yang Two Pillars (``Jingi Hoden'') {{Sfn|Kitabatake Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}} * {{ill|lt=Izanagi|Q813858|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagison|1=Izanagi}} Zainmine, {{ill|lt=Izanami|Q682306|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanagison|1=Izanami}}zainmine (“Hitachikuni 28 Shrines”) {{Sfn|Kitabatake Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}} * Yomine{{ill|lt=Hannyas|Q9285919|WD=Q9285919|lt=Haniyama Hikokami|1=Haniyasu-hiko and Haniyasu-hime}}, Inmine{{ill|lt=Hannyas|Q9285919|WD=Q9285919|lt=Haniyama Himekami|1=Haniyasu-hiko and Haniyasu-hime}} ("{{ill|lt=Divine Name Book Research|Q11588824|WD=Q11588824|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō Studies}}") {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}} * The enshrined deity is unknown, and legend says, ``Izanagison Zaiyomine, Izashoson Zainmine, commonly known as Tsukuba Daimyojin'' ({{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}'12 ({{ill|lt=1879|Q7783|WD=Q7783|1=1879}}) ``Mount Tsukuba Shrine Detailed Record'') {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}}After that, based on the records in the Six Kingdoms History, in January 1942 ({{ill|lt=1909|Q2057|WD=Q2057|1=1909}}), the names of the deities enshrined were determined to be ``Tsukuba Otokojin'' and ``Tsukuba Goddess.''{{Sfn|Meiji Shrine Magazine Materials|1912}}. Then, in {{ill|lt=Taisho|Q329174|WD=Q329174|1=Taishō era}}11 ({{ill|lt=1922|Q2165|WD=Q2165|1=1922}}), it was decided that ``Tsukuba Man God/Tsukuba Goddess'' should be written with ``Iza Nōson/Iza Shoson.''{{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}}. Furthermore, the origin and history of the tradition of Izaninoson and Izashozon is not clear. === History === === Founding === Founding date is unknown. Mount Tsukuba is said to have been revered since the time when people began living in the Kanto Plain, as it is so impressive that it is contrasted with {{ill|lt=Mt. Fuji|Q39231|WD=Q39231|1=Mount Fuji}} in the ``{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|WD=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}''. According to the shrine biography (``Mt. Tsukuba Engi''), {{jalink|domestic production|Q3545163} written by Iza Nōson and Iza Shokuson in {{ill|lt=Kojiki|Q813031|WD=Q813031|1=Kojiki}}. }} "{{ill|lt=Onogoro Island|Q2985158|WD=Q2985158|lt=Onokoro Island|1=Onogoro Island}}" is said to correspond to Mt. Tsukuba {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. In addition, in "Shiririn Kayosho" ({{ill|lt=Nanbokucho Period (Japan)|Q264012|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho Period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}), Mt. Tsukuba is said to be the sacred mountain where {{ill|lt=Amaterasu Omikami|UNKNOWN|lt=Amaterasu Omikami}} descended. (era name)|Q1373146|Culture}} ({{ill|lt=1804|Q6894|WD=Q6894|1=1804}}-{{ill|lt=1818|Q6964|WD=Q6964|1=1818}}) "Kiji" also tells about the transfer of the same god from Tsukuba to Ise.Regarding the ritual clans, since Tsukuba no Mikoto (Tsukuba Mikoto, Tsukuba Mikoto), who appears in "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki", was appointed as the first {{ill|lt=Tsukuba Kunizo|Q11602846|WD=Q11602846|1=Tsukuba Kunizo}}, it is said that Tsukuba Kunizo served in unison with rituals and politicsThe founding tradition of the nearby {{ill|lt=Serikage Shrine|Q17228464|WD=Q17228464|1=Kokage Shrine}} (Kami-gun, Tsukuba City) also says that during the reign of {{ill|lt=Emperor Seimu|Q316672|WD=Q316672|1=Emperor Seimu}}, Tsukuba Kunizo's Akishiro-no-Mikoto enshrined Tsukuba Okami. . Many ancient tombs remain at the foot of Mt. Tsukuba, among which {{ill|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus (Tsukuba City)|Q17218702|WD=Q17218702|lt=Hachimanzuka Tumulus|1=Hachimanzuka-kofun}} (Numata, Tsukuba City) is thought to be a Tsukuba Kuni-zukuri tomb.{{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=414}}. The current main part of Tsukubasan Shrine is located around the worship hall, but the worship hall was built in 1875 on the site of Chuzenji Temple. Therefore, the "original Mt. Tsukuba Shrine" refers to the "Nantai Mt. Shrine and Nyotai Mt. Shrine". Tsukuba Shrine|1984|p=412}}. . Also, although the date of its establishment is unknown, the ruins of Rokusho Shrine in Usui, Tsukuba City (currently a closed shrine) were the satomiya of both shrines (see section {{ill|lt=#Related locations|UNKNOWN|lt=Related locations}}). === Outline === ==== From the Nara period to the Heian period ==== ``{{ill|lt=Manyoshu|Q834321|WD=Q834321|1=Man'yōshū}}'' from the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|WD=Q189178|1=Nara period}} includes 25 poems from Tsukuba, and Mt. Tsukuba is said to have been the mountain representing {{ill|lt=Hitachi Province|Q1055353|WD=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}. Also, from the end of the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|WD=Q189178|1=Nara period}} to the beginning of the {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292|1=Heian period}}, the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hosso sect|1=UNKNOWN}} The monk {{ill|lt=Tokuichi|Q7813728|WD=Q7813728|1=Tokuitsu}} opened Tsukubasanji Temple, later Tsukubasan Chisokuin Chuzenji Temple {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}}. As a result, {{ill|lt=Shinto-Buddhist syncretism|Q2279088|WD=Q2279088|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and Mt. Tsukuba developed into one of the leading {{ill|lt=Shugendo|Q1483875|WD=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}} dojos {{Sfn|Chuzenji Ruins (Heibonsha)|1982}} (for details, see the {{ill|lt=#Chuzenji|UNKNOWN|lt=Chuzenji}} section). During this period of syncretization of Shinto and Buddhism, it was also called ``Tsukuba Ryodaigongen'' (Ryobe Gongen).In the {{ill|lt=Rokukokushi|Q1151168|WD=Q1151168|lt=Kokushi|1=Rikkokushi}}, there is an article that says that in ancient times, in {{ill|lt=Honin|Q1373070|WD=Q1373070|1=Kōnin (era)}} 14 ({{ill|lt=823|Q29944|WD=Q29944|1=823}}) , the Tsukuba deity, which was lower than the Junior Fifth Rank, was made {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=government shrine|1=UNKNOWN}}. With the subsequent investiture of {{ill|lt=Divine Rank|Q11591025|WD=Q11591025|1=Shinkai (divine rank)}}, {{ill|lt=Jōkan (Japan)|Q1075635|WD=Q1075635|lt=Jōkan|1=Jōgan}}13 ({{ill|lt=871|Q24754|WD=Q24754|1=871}}), Tsukuba Ogami rose to Jusanmi (Junior Third Rank), and in Jogan 16 ({{ill|lt=874|Q23843|WD=Q23843|1=874}}) , Tsukuba Goddess rose to Jushini-Ji (or Sei-shii Shimi-ge <{{ill|lt=#Divine rank|UNKNOWN|lt=described later}}>).{{ill|lt=Extension (era name)|Q1327274|WD=Q1327274|lt=Extension|1=Enchō}} "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|WD=Q30470|1=927}}) Tsukuba District, Hitachi Province. In {{ill|lt=Hitachi-kuni|Q1055353|WD=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Tsukuba-gun|Q7850092|WD=Q7850092|1=Tsukuba District, Ibaraki}} there are "Tsukubasan Shrine Niza Ichiza Meishindai It is listed as the only {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shikinaisha|1=UNKNOWN}} shrine in Tsukuba County, of which {{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}} is said to be the Tsukuba Man God, and the small shrine is said to be the Tsukuba Goddess {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. After that, in {{ill|lt=Jisho|Q1194671|WD=Q1194671|1=Jishō}} 4th year ({{ill|lt=1180|Q19702|WD=Q19702|1=1180}}), is said to have reached the rank of Shoichi. ==== From Kamakura period to Edo period ==== In the early {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, {{ill|lt=Tomoie Hatta|Q11391665|WD=Q11391665|1=Tomoie Hatta}} of {{ill|lt=Hitachi Province|Q1055353|WD=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Guo|Q1141023|WD=Q1141023|1=Shugo}} ({{ill|lt=Oda clan|Q11463150|WD=Q11463150|1=Oda clan}}'s son Hachiro Tameji inherited the name of Tsukuba Kunizo and became Tsukuba {{ill|lt=Betto|Q2900274|WD=Q2900274|1=Bettō}} {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The descendants of this Tameji Tsukuba (Myogen) thereafter called themselves the Tsukuba clan, and were the enshriners of the Tsukuba deity as well as the charge of Chuzenji temple {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The trends in the Middle Ages are not clear, but in {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185|1=Keichō}}5 ({{ill|lt=1600|Q6720|WD=Q6720|1=1600}}) Until the Tsukuba clan was removed by Kawaieyasu|Q171977}}, the Tsukuba deity, Chuzenji, is said to have been under the control of the Tsukuba clan {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, the {{ill|lt=Edo Shogunate|Q205662|WD=Q205662|lt=Bakufu|1=Tokugawa shogunate}} fiercely protected Chuzenji, many temples and pagodas were erected within the grounds of Chuzenji, and the character of Mt. Tsukuba changed from a co-existence of Shinto and Buddhism to a sacred place centered on Buddhism.{{Sfn|Mount Tsukuba Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Despite this patronage of Chuzen-ji Temple, the shadow of Tsukuba-kami was weak, and the form of Tsukuba-kami's enshrinement during this period is not clear {{Sfn|Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (National History)|1988}} (for trends in the Edo period, see section {{ill|lt=#Chuzenji|UNKNOWN|lt=Chuzenji}}).At the end of the Edo period, the Tenguto raised an army in the first year of {{ill|lt=Genji|Q1325419|WD=Q1325419|1=Genji era}} ({{ill|lt=1864|Q7704|WD=Q7704|1=1864}}), and {{ja link|Tenguto Rebellion|Q1040831}} ({{ill|lt=Tenguto Rebellion#Mt.Tsukuba Raising of Arms|Q1040831|WD=Q1040831|lt=Mt. Tsukuba Incident|1=Mito Rebellion}}). ==== After Meiji ====

{{Harv|Kitabatake Tsukubayama Shrine|1984|p=414}}. === Precincts === The precincts of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine are 354 {{ill|lt=hectare|Q35852|WD=Q35852|1=Hectare}} on the south side of Mt. Tsukuba, more than 270 meters above sea level. . The main shrine is located on the summit of Mt. Nantai and Mt. Nyotai of Mt. Tsukuba, and there is a shrine on the mountainside where you can worship from a distance. === Tsukuba Yamanaka === [[File:Tsukubasan-jinja nantaisan-honden.JPG|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Nantaiyama Main Hall}}]] [[File:Mount Tsukuba Shrine on top.jpg|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Nyotaiyama Main Hall}}]] '''Mt. Nyotai Main Hall'' was built in {{ill|lt=Showa|Q327567|WD=Q327567|1=Shōwa era}}30 ({{ill|lt=1955|Q18577|WD=Q18577|1=1955}}), '''Mt. The main hall''' was renovated in 1979 ({{ill|lt=1979|Q2484|WD=Q2484|1=1979}}), and both are Ikkensha {{ill|lt=Ryuzo|Q210684|WD=Q210684|1=Nagare-zukuri}}. At the summit of Mt. Nantai, there is a joint observatory with {{ill|lt=University of Tsukuba|Q743615|WD=Q743615|1=University of Tsukuba}} {{ill|lt=Joint Meteorological Observatory of Tsukubasan Shrine and University of Tsukuba Computational Science Research Center|Q11602877|WD=Q11602877|1=Meteorological Station of the Mt. Tsukuba Shrine & Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba}} (facilities and land owned by Tsukubasan Shrine Hayashi (2007): p. 7. Nishimura (2010): p. 559. ) At the summit of Mt. Nyotai, there is a shrine awarding place and Ama no Ukihashi (rebuilt in April 2009). The saddle between the two peaks is called ``Miyukigahara.'' About 300 meters to Mt. Nantai and about 600 meters to Mt. Nyotai. The Tsukuba Cable Car's Tsukuba Sancho Station is located here, and there are many souvenir shops and restaurants.In addition, in the mountains there is also the "Men and Women River," which is famous as the subject of {{ill|lt=Emperor Yozei|Q349280|WD=Q349280|lt=Yoseiin|1=Emperor Yōzei}}'s poem {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ogura Hyakunin Isshu|1=UNKNOWN}}. (Ibaraki Prefecture) In addition to the source of the Minanogawa River, there is also the Shihosugi Cedar. There are many sacred stones, strangely shaped rocks, and famous trees, such as the {{ill|lt=cedar|Q147388|WD=Q147388|1=Cryptomeria}} named ``Cedar'' (near the headwaters of the Men and Women River), which is estimated to be 800 years old, ``Benkei Seven Returns'', ``Mother's Womb Passing'', and ``Gama Stone''. These rocky areas were once used as a dojo for {{ill|lt=Shugendo|Q1483875|WD=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}}, and Mt. Tsukuba meditation is still performed as a Shinto ritual. === Around the shrine === [[File:Tsukubasan-jinja zuishinmon.JPG|thumb|160px|right|{{Center|Zuishinmon
(Tsukuba City designated cultural property)}}]] [[File:Tsukubasan Shrine Oshinbashi Front.JPG|thumb|160px|right|{{Center|Shinbashi
(Ibaraki Prefecture Designated Cultural Property)}}]] A {{ill|lt=monzen town|Q10564515|WD=Q10564515|1=Monzen-machi}} is formed around the worship hall, which forms the main part of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. However, before the Meiji era, this area was a sacred place centered on Buddhism, with Chuzenji as its main temple {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}, but when Chuzenji was abolished after the Meiji Restoration, it was revived as a shrine and a worship hall was built.``The Hall of Worship'' was built in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}8 ({{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|WD=Q7764|1=1875}}). The plaque on the front, "Tsukuba Shrine," is written by {{ill|lt=Prince Komatsunomiya Akihito|Q712627|WD=Q712627|1=Prince Komatsu Akihito}} and engraved by {{ill|lt=Koun Takamura|Q2080344|WD=Q2080344|1=Takamura Kōun}} from Famous Places Guide (Mito Transportation Office, 1927), page 3. . Before the Meiji period, there was the main hall (Omido) of Chuzenji Temple at this location, but after the Omido was abolished due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, a new one was built {{Sfn|Tsukubasan Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The foundation stone remains in front of the worship hall, reminiscent of the Chuzenji temple {{Sfn|Kitabatake Tsukubasan Shrine|1984|p=418}}. Furthermore, Omido has been rebuilt as {{ill|lt=Omido (Tsukuba City)|Q11435427|WD=Q11435427|lt=Omido|1=Ōmi-dō}} of the {{ill|lt=Toyoyama School of Shingon Sect|Q3077351|WD=Q3077351|1=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha}} Omido Church to the southwest of the worship hall.The ``Zuishinmon'' (Zuishinmon) built in front of the worship hall is a tower gate with a width of 5 x 2 shaku and a depth of 3 x 3, making it one of the largest in Ibaraki Prefecture. . It was originally donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in {{ill|lt=Kanei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913|1=Kan'ei}}10 ({{ill|lt=1633|Q6870|WD=Q6870|1=1633}}), but {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Horeki|1=UNKNOWN}} It was burnt down in 4th year ({{ill|lt=1754|Q7623|WD=Q7623|1=1754}}), and although it was rebuilt, it was burnt down again in 4th year of Meiwa ({{ill|lt=1767|Q7672|WD=Q7672|1=1767}}). The current tower gate was rebuilt in {{ill|lt=Bunka (era name)|Q1373146|WD=Q1373146|lt=Bunka|1=Bunka}}8 ({{ill|lt=1811|Q6928|WD=Q6928|1=1811}}). During the {{ill|lt=syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism|Q2279088|WD=Q2279088|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} period, Nio statues (Vajra Rikishi statues) were enshrined there as ``Niomon'', but after {{ill|lt=Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|Q1970535|WD=Q1970535|1=Shinbutsu bunri}}, it was called ``Zuishinmon''. During the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, the Nio statue was floated down the Sakuragawa River on a raft and taken to Tofukuji Temple in Matsuzuka, Tsukuba City. For this reason, it is now called ``Nagare Nio.'' Takayoshi Nishitani. The sacred mountain of Mt. Tsukuba and Tokuichi Daishi: Chisoku-in Chuzenji and Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. Ibaraki Prefecture Local Culture Honor Society, 2012. At the current Zuishinmon gate, the Zuishin statue of {{ill|lt=Yamato Takeru|Q461258|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}} (Yamato Takeru no Mikoto) is enshrined on the left side of the shrine, and on the right side is the Zuishin statue of {{ill|lt=Yamato Takeru|Q461258|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}}. This Zuishinmon gate has been designated as a cultural property designated by Tsukuba City.Beside the Zuishinmon gate is the Koyo Shonin Five Ring Tower. This is the only temple-related {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=doto pagoda|1=UNKNOWN}} that remains at Tsukubasan Shrine, which was spared from destruction and relocation during {{ill|lt=Haitbutsu Kishaku|Q702298|WD=Q702298|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} in the early Meiji period. One theory is that Kotan was the son of {{ill|lt=Hidetada Tokugawa|Q314464|WD=Q314464|1=Tokugawa Hidetada}}'s wet nurse, and entered the Betsto Chisoku-in temple on Mt. Tsukuba in 1611. {{ill|lt=Osaka no Siege|Q475780|WD=Q475780|lt=Osaka Summer Siege and Winter Siege|1=Siege of Osaka}} He is said to have served in the army and prayed for victory, and is said to have died on December 19, 1624, {{ill|lt=Kanei|Q1192913|WD=Q1192913|1=Kan'ei}}{{Cite book|Japanese book|title=Kanto's Famous Mountain, Mt. Tsukuba, Guide to Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|publisher=Mt. Tsukuba Shrine|year=2008|page=40}}.The ``Shinkyo Bridge'' built on the approach is {{ill|lt=Gabled|Q13308575|WD=Q13308575|1=Kirizuma-style}} with a thatched roof, 1 ken in frontage and 4 ken in depth, and is a sled bridge in the {{ill|lt=Azuchi-Momoyama period|Q319531|WD=Q319531|1=Azuchi–Momoyama period}} style. {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Shinbashi}}. It is said to have been donated by the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1633, and was renovated by the fifth shogun {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi|Q313745|WD=Q313745|1=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi}} in {{ill|lt=Genroku|Q1325001|WD=Q1325001|1=Genroku}}15 ({{ill|lt=1702|Q6819|WD=Q6819|1=1702}}). During the Spring and Autumn Gozachange Festival, mikoshi and attendants cross here {{Sfn|Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education|Shinbashi}}. Worshipers are normally prohibited from crossing the bridge, and are only allowed during the Spring and Autumn Gozagae Festival and the February Toshikoshi Festival . This Shinbashi bridge is designated as a cultural property of Ibaraki Prefecture. A bronze statue of {{ill|lt=Koshiro Fujita|Q11288247|WD=Q11288247|1=Fujita Kishirō}} is erected near the entrance to the shrine. Koshiro Fujita was the fourth son of {{ill|lt=Toko Fujita|Q6564466|WD=Q6564466|1=Fujita Tōko}} and was the leader of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tenguto|1=UNKNOWN}} Tsukuba faction that raised an army at Mt. Tsukuba on March 27, 1864 (May 2, 1864). A plaque by Mito local historians Ohsui Ando and Saburo Yumene was installed near the statue in 1990.Additionally, Kasuga Shrine, Hie Shrine, and Itsukushima Shrine, which were built as guardian shrines of Chuzenji Temple, remain today as the final shrines of Mt. Tsukuba Shrine (see section {{ill|lt=#terminal shrine|UNKNOWN|lt=terminal shrine}}). Near Kasuga Hie Shrine stands a variety of camphor tree {{ill|lt=Marubagus|Q24868661|WD=Q24868661|1=Cinnamomum camphora var. rotundifolia}} (Marubagusu), which is designated as a natural monument by Tsukuba City, and near the tower gate stands a large cedar tree that is about 800 years old and 32 meters tall. In addition, within the precincts are the grave of {{ill|lt=Masakatsu Kusunoki|Q11541195|WD=Q11541195|1=Kusunoki Masakatsu}}, the grandson of {{ill|lt=Masashige Kusunoki|Q382234|WD=Q382234|1=Kusunoki Masashige}}, and the space egg that was exhibited at the {{ill|lt=International Science and Technology Exposition|Q2312924|WD=Q2312924|1=Expo 85 (Tsukuba, Japan)}} (Science Expo). Although normally closed to the public, there is also a storehouse that collects various materials provided to pray for and express gratitude for the success of each pavilion (it was opened to the public for a limited time in July 2006). Additionally, monuments of 25 Tsukuba poems from the Manyoshu have been erected around Mt. Tsukuba, including Mt. Tsukuba Shrine. In addition, at the former Rokusho Shrine (Usui, Tsukuba City: Tsukubasan Shrine Motosato Shrine) and Rokusho Shrine (Izumi, Tsukuba City), the ``Rokusho'', which includes the above-mentioned four sessha shrines, was enshrined in addition to the two deities of Tsukuba Men and Women.
